case_title: Fictional: the St Ilven hospital in Varnetsa
question: Did the Calvaran strike on the St Ilven hospital on 13 August 2025 violate the protection owed to civilian medical units under the law of international armed conflict?
facts: An international armed conflict has existed since March 2025 between the Republic of Calvaro and the Federation of Drennick, both parties to the four Geneva Conventions of 1949, Additional Protocol I and the Rome Statute. St Ilven Hospital in the town of Varnetsa is a civilian hospital recognised by the Drennick authorities and marked with the red cross emblem. From 2 August 2025, after Drennick forces withdrew into Varnetsa, a Drennick artillery observation team occupied the hospital's top floor and from there directed artillery fire onto Calvaran positions; a heavy machine gun mounted on the hospital roof fired on Calvaran troops; and the basement was used to store artillery ammunition. On 9 August Calvaran forces warned, by radio broadcast on frequencies used by Drennick forces, by leaflets, and through a delegate of the International Committee of the Red Cross, that unless all military use of the hospital ceased within 48 hours it would lose its protection and be attacked, and offered a safe corridor for the evacuation of patients and staff. The military use continued: the roof machine gun fired on Calvaran troops on 10 and 11 August. Between 9 and 12 August all patients and medical staff left through the corridor, and on 12 August the hospital director told the ICRC delegate that no patients or medical staff remained in the building. On 13 August Calvaran aircraft struck the top floor and roof with two guided munitions, chosen to avoid the lower floors. The strike killed two Drennick soldiers on the roof and destroyed the top floor. No civilians were in the building.
holding: Authored ground truth for a fictional case; no tribunal has ruled on it. No. Protection of a civilian medical unit ceases when it is used, outside its humanitarian function, to commit acts harmful to the enemy, after a warning setting a reasonable time-limit has remained unheeded (GC IV Art. 19 for civilian hospitals; AP I Art. 13(1) for civilian medical units; customary Rule 28). Directing artillery fire, firing a machine gun and storing ammunition are acts harmful to the enemy and none falls within the exceptions in GC IV Art. 19(2) or AP I Art. 13(2). A warning naming a 48-hour time-limit was given through several channels and went unheeded. With patients and staff evacuated and munitions chosen to limit the damage, the strike involved no incidental civilian harm, and the precautions required by Art. 57 were taken. The strike did not violate the protection owed to the hospital under GC IV Arts. 18–19 or AP I Arts. 12–13.
confidence_reasoning: The conclusion rests on settled treaty law (GC IV Art. 19, AP I Arts. 12–13) and a factual record that meets every statutory condition for loss of protection and for a precautionary attack. The absence of any objection or competing argument eliminates evidentiary uncertainty. A confidence of 0.95 reflects that the only residual risk would be an unforeseen judicial interpretation narrowing 'acts harmful to the enemy' or 'reasonable time limit', which is not suggested by the retrieved authorities.

verdict.conclusion: No. The Calvaran strike on 13 August 2025 did not violate the protection owed to civilian medical units under the law of international armed conflict. The hospital lost its protection under Article 19 of the Fourth Geneva Convention and Article 13 of Additional Protocol I because it was used for acts harmful to the enemy (artillery observation, machine-gun fire, ammunition storage) and a due warning with a reasonable 48-hour time limit was given on 9 August and remained unheeded as military use continued on 10–11 August. By 12 August all patients and staff had evacuated, and the 13 August strike was directed only at the military objectives on the roof and top floor using precision munitions, with no civilians present. The attack therefore complied with the conditions for lawful targeting after loss of protection and with the principles of distinction and precaution. No objections were filed to challenge this analysis. The surviving arguments (arg_d6e6618d, arg_7742efcb, arg_4b48b83e) are fully supported by the cited treaty provisions. Confidence is high because the treaty text, the factual record, and the absence of any counter-argument all align.
verdict.reasoning: The three arguments presented establish that (1) the hospital was used for acts harmful to the enemy within the meaning of GC IV Art. 19 and AP I Art. 13, (2) the 9 August warning satisfied the requirement of a reasonable time limit and was unheeded, and (3) once protection ceased, the strike was a lawful attack on a military objective conducted with feasible precautions. The cited treaty articles (gc_iv/art.19, ap_i/art.13, ap_i/art.12) are all resolved in the corpus and directly support each step. No objections were raised, so no rulings are required.

arguments.claim: The protection afforded to St Ilven Hospital under the Geneva Conventions ceased because the hospital was used to commit acts harmful to the enemy.
arguments.reasoning: Article 19 of the Fourth Geneva Convention expressly states that protection does not cease unless a civilian hospital is used for acts harmful to the enemy. The occupation of the top floor as an artillery observation post, the firing of a heavy machine gun from the roof, and the storage of artillery ammunition in the basement are clearly acts of combat outside any humanitarian function. These uses are not among the exceptions listed in Additional Protocol I, which only exclude light personal defence weapons, pickets, small arms taken from the wounded, and the presence of combatants for medical reasons. Consequently, the hospital lost its protected status before the attack.
